prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I was born in minutes in a roadside kitchen a skillet whispering my name. I was born to rainwater and lye; I was born across the river where I was borrowed with clothespins, a harrow tooth, broadsides sewn in my shoes. I returned, though it please you, through no fault of my own, pockets filled with coffee grounds and eggshells. I was born still and superstitious; I bore an unexpected burden. I gave birth, I gave blessing, I gave rise to suspicion. I was born abandoned outdoors in the heat-shaped air, air drifting like spirits and old windows. I was born a fraction and a cipher and a ledger entry; I was an index of first lines when I was born. I was born waist-deep stubborn in the water crying ain’t I a woman and a brother I was born to this hall of mirrors, this horror story I was born with a prologue of references, pursued by mosquitoes and thieves, I was born passing off the problem of the twentieth century: I was born. I read minds before I could read fishes and loaves; I walked a piece of the way alone before I was born.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: I was born

outputs.L1:
I was born in minutes, in a roadside kitchen, a skillet whispering my name. I was born to rainwater and lye; I was born across the river, where I was borrowed with clothespins, a harrow tooth, and broadsides sewn into my shoes. I returned, though it may please you, through no fault of my own, my pockets filled with coffee grounds and eggshells.

I was born still and superstitious; I bore an unexpected burden. I gave birth, I gave blessing, I gave rise to suspicion. I was born abandoned outdoors in the heat-shaped air, air drifting like spirits and old windows. I was born a fraction, a cipher, and a ledger entry; I was an index of first lines when I was born.

I was born waist-deep and stubborn in the water, crying, “Ain’t I a woman and a brother?” I was born to this hall of mirrors, this horror story. I was born with a prologue of references, pursued by mosquitoes and thieves. I was born passing off the problem of the twentieth century: I was born. I read minds before I could read fishes and loaves; I walked a piece of the way alone before I was born.
outputs.L2:
My beginning came in a matter of minutes, in a kitchen beside the road, while a pan seemed to murmur my name. I came from rainwater mixed with lye; I came into being beyond the river, where I had been taken on loan along with clothespins, the tooth of a harrow, and printed sheets stitched into my shoes. I came back, if that suits you, through no doing of mine, with my pockets packed with coffee grounds and eggshells.

I entered the world motionless and full of omens; I carried a weight no one expected. I delivered life, offered benediction, and became the source of doubt. I came into being deserted outside, in air bent by heat, air moving like ghosts and antique panes of glass. I began as a portion, a secret mark, a notation in an account book; at birth, I was a catalog of opening lines.

I came into the world planted waist-high in water, defiant, shouting, “Ain’t I a woman and a brother?” I was made for this chamber of reflections, this tale of terror. I arrived with a preface made of citations, chased by mosquitoes and robbers. I was born handing onward the question of the twentieth century: I existed. Before I knew how to read fishes and loaves, I could read thoughts; before my birth, I had already traveled part of the road by myself.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents birth not as a single, fixed event, but as something multiple, shifting, and symbolic. They describe being born in many places and in many forms, moving between ordinary domestic images and strange, surreal origins. This mixture of the familiar and the uncanny suggests that the speaker’s identity cannot be contained by one birthplace, one body, or one simple story. Birth becomes expansive: it happens in homes, in histories, in language, and in the imagination.

From the moment of birth, the speaker carries the weight of difficult histories. Hardship, abandonment, suspicion, and burden are not experiences that arrive later in life; they are present from the beginning. The speaker seems to inherit pain before having the chance to choose anything for themselves. Their existence is shaped by forces larger than the individual—family histories, social judgment, poverty, displacement, and systems that mark certain bodies as vulnerable or unwanted.

The speaker’s identity is also shown as fragmented and reduced into impersonal forms. They become records, references, fractions, and ciphers, as though they have been classified rather than fully seen. This language suggests a world that tries to catalogue, measure, and define the speaker while also erasing their humanity. Instead of being recognized as a whole person, the speaker is broken into data, documents, labels, and traces. Their selfhood survives, but it survives under pressure from systems that turn living people into categories.

The text also invokes larger struggles over race, gender, and humanity. Echoes of the phrase “ain’t I a woman” recall Sojourner Truth’s challenge to racist and sexist ideas about womanhood, while the reference to “the problem of the twentieth century” evokes W. E. B. Du Bois’s famous statement about the color line. These allusions place the speaker’s personal birth within a broader historical and political context. The speaker is not only telling an individual story; they are speaking from within legacies of racial oppression, gendered exclusion, and the fight to be recognized as fully human.

Ultimately, birth in this piece is both literal and ongoing. It marks the beginning of life, but it also becomes a repeated process of becoming, remembering, enduring, and surviving. The speaker is born into memory as much as into the world, carrying inherited struggles while continuing to move forward. Birth is therefore not simply an origin point; it is a journey through oppression and resilience, through erasure and self-claiming, through the past that shapes the speaker and the survival that allows them to keep being born.
outputs.L4:
I was born more than once.

I was born first in a room where the air was thick with waiting, where women moved softly and men stood outside pretending not to be afraid. I was born into hands that had held other children, into sheets washed thin by years of use, into a cry that was mine and not mine, because it carried the sound of everyone who had cried before me. I was born with a name already hovering over me, a name chosen, argued over, inherited, shortened, misspelled, and sometimes withheld.

I was born into a family, but also into a history. Before I could speak, I had been spoken for. Before I could walk, paths had been laid beneath my feet. There were stories waiting for me like old furniture in a dark house: stories of mothers, fathers, grandmothers, strangers, fields, kitchens, borders, ships, hospitals, churches, graves. Some of them were offered to me tenderly. Some were hidden. Some were denied so fiercely that their absence became another kind of presence.

I was born with other people’s memories in my mouth.

I was born beneath a sky that had seen everything and explained nothing. I was born into weather, into hunger, into lullabies, into warnings. I was born into the sound of doors closing, locks turning, footsteps pausing outside. I was born into suspicion: the suspicion of neighbors, officials, lovers, enemies, and sometimes even kin. I was born into the knowledge that a body can be read before it is known, judged before it acts, named before it answers.

I was born a child, but not an innocent one. No child is innocent in a world that has already made decisions about them. I was born with skin, with sex, with blood, with a face that resembled some people and troubled others. I was born into categories I did not invent, into boxes older than my bones. I was born into the question of what I was, who I belonged to, what could be expected from me, what could be taken from me, what I might become if no one interfered.

I was born in the shadow of race, though no shadow announced itself honestly. It entered through glances, through laws, through jokes, through silences at the table. It entered through the way people said “your people” and meant something both intimate and accusing. It entered through the records kept and the records burned, through the neighborhoods divided, through the names changed at ports and courthouses, through the careful training of children to lower their eyes or raise their chins.

I was born in the shadow of gender, too. Before I understood my own body, the world had begun instructing it. Sit this way. Speak this way. Do not want too much. Do not be too loud. Be soft. Be strong. Be pleasing. Be careful. Be grateful. I was born into hands that measured me, dressed me, corrected me, praised me for obedience, punished me for hunger. I was born into the old theater of men and women, where everyone is given a costume and told it is skin.

I was born among the living and the dead.

The dead were not gone. They leaned in corners. They sat at the foot of the bed. They appeared in photographs with blurred eyes and stiff collars. They lived in recipes, scars, debts, diseases, songs, and habits of fear. They lived in the way my mother folded cloth, in the way my father stared out of windows, in the way no one said certain names after dark. I was born into their unfinished sentences. I was born as their evidence.

I was born in fragments. A hand. A street. A red dress. A broken cup. A field after rain. A train whistle. A locked drawer. A woman laughing too loudly. A man refusing to answer. A child hiding under the table. A church bell. A hospital bracelet. A stain no washing could remove. These things came to me before meaning did. They gathered around me and waited until I was old enough to be haunted.

I was born into inheritance, but inheritance was not treasure. It was not only land, silver, stories, or a family Bible with names written in fading ink. It was also debt. It was also shame. It was also pride sharpened into a weapon. It was the burden of explaining oneself to people who had already decided not to understand. It was the obligation to remember what others wished forgotten, and the temptation to forget what hurt too much to carry.

I was born from a mother, but also from every refusal that allowed her to live long enough to bear me. I was born from her endurance, from her fear, from the bargains she made with the world. I was born from her body, yes, but also from the bodies before hers, bodies bent over work, bodies watched, bodies desired, bodies punished, bodies that survived by becoming quiet or clever or invisible. I was born from all the ways they did not die.

I was born in a house, and then I was born again when I left it.

I was born when I learned my name could sound different in different mouths. I was born when I saw myself reflected in a window at night and did not recognize the face looking back. I was born when someone loved me and called it rescue. I was born when someone feared me and called it reason. I was born when I discovered that belonging was not a door one walked through once, but a threshold guarded over and over again.

I was born in the country that claimed me and questioned me. It gave me documents, songs, schoolbooks, flags, and warnings. It taught me its history in clean paragraphs while the older history breathed beneath the floorboards. It said freedom and meant patience. It said equality and meant later. It said home and meant prove it. I was born into that contradiction, into the space between promise and practice, between the official story and the story whispered in kitchens after the children were supposed to be asleep.

I was born with a body that could be touched, harmed, desired, doubted, celebrated, misread. I was born with a body that remembered even when I did not. It remembered fear in the shoulders, grief in the stomach, anger in the hands. It remembered being watched. It remembered being told to smile. It remembered running, though I had never run from anything. It remembered danger as if danger were an ancestor.

I was born into language, but language was broken. Words arrived chipped and stained. Some words had to be swallowed. Some could not be translated. Some were used against me until I learned to turn them around. I was born into a language that could bless and wound in the same breath. I learned that to speak was to risk being misunderstood, and to remain silent was to risk disappearing.

I was born many times in silence.

I was born in the silence after an insult. In the silence before a verdict. In the silence of women who knew more than they were permitted to say. In the silence of men who mistook feeling for weakness. In the silence of archives where no one had bothered to write down the lives that made my life possible. I was born in the blank spaces, the missing pages, the torn-out names.

And still I was born.

That is the miracle and the accusation. I was born despite calculation, despite neglect, despite the long machinery of exclusion. I was born into a world that had prepared a place for me and also denied that place existed. I was born as proof that survival is not simple. It is not pure triumph. It is bruised, compromised, stubborn, communal. No one is born alone, no matter how solitary the first cry sounds. A birth gathers the living, the dead, the unwilling, the forgotten, the guilty, the hopeful. It opens a door and releases everything that has been waiting behind it.

I was born, and with me came questions.

Who made me possible? Who paid for my arrival? Whose pain became my shelter? Whose name do I carry? Whose silence protects me, and whose silence condemns me? What history moves in my blood without my consent? What must I keep? What must I refuse? What must I transform so that those born after me inherit something other than fear?

I was born not as a beginning, but as a continuation.

I was born layered: child and ancestor, witness and evidence, body and memory, self and multitude. I was born into suspicion, but also into song. I was born into burden, but also into breath. I was born among ruins, yet the fact of my birth was not ruin. It was a claim. It was a refusal to vanish. It was a contested belonging, yes, but belonging nonetheless.

I was born, and the world did not know what to do with me.

So I began to live.
outputs.L5:
I was born into a world full of possibilities, where every day offered something new to learn and experience. From the very beginning, life became a journey shaped by family, memories, challenges, and dreams. The place where I was born is more than just a location; it is the starting point of my story. It holds the first sounds I heard, the first faces I saw, and the first moments that quietly helped shape who I would become.

As time passed, I began to understand that being born is not only about entering the world. It is also about growing, discovering, and becoming. Every person has a unique beginning, and each beginning carries meaning. When I say, “I was born,” I am not only talking about a date or a place. I am talking about the first chapter of a life that continues to unfold.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem that repeats the phrase “I was born” and weaves in fragmented allusions to African American literature, folklore, archives, and birth narratives.
counterfactuals.output:
I was born in the margin where the census taker’s ink ran out. I was born between two names, one swallowed by salt, one pinned to a county ledger with a rusted nail. I was born when the midwife washed her hands in moonlight and said the child has already been here, already knocking from inside the door.

I was born in a sack of waters, caul-bright, conjure-eyed, with a rabbit foot of thunder under my tongue. I was born hearing the old people say hush, hush, don’t let the river learn your true name. I was born in the story of the flying Africans, in the field after the field after the field, where the hoe leaned against heaven and refused to apologize.

I was born in a library basement, in a box marked MISCELLANEOUS NEGRO MATERIALS, beneath church fans, funeral programs, photographs with the faces silvering away. I was born from a receipt for a body, from a bill of sale that tried to spell mother as property and failed. I was born in the crease of a freedom paper folded so many times it became a wing.

I was born with a blues note for a spine. I was born under a porch where a woman was laughing so hard God had to sit down. I was born in the hot comb’s hiss, in the kitchen’s cathedral, in the skillet’s blackened memory. I was born where the sweetgrass basket remembers the hand, where the quilt talks in triangles, where the bottle tree drinks blue ghosts at dawn.

I was born in a room full of women saying breathe, baby, breathe, while outside the night patrol counted stars like suspects. I was born feet-first into a psalm, head-first into trouble. I was born and the cord was cut with a knife that had skinned okra, opened letters, defended a doorway, and split a peach in June.

I was born in the mouth of a griot who had lost the village but not the drum. I was born in a folktale where Brer Rabbit tricks the grave into laughing. I was born in John’s de conkeroo, in High John’s pocket, in the root doctor’s jar labeled for sorrow but filled with red clay and sunrise. I was born from a black cat’s shadow crossing a baptismal pool.

I was born in a sentence that kept breaking its chains. I was born where the invisible man flickered in the electric dark, where the weary singer asked about dreams deferred, where a woman watched God and found a horizon inside herself. I was born in a beloved house, in a room numbered by haunting, in the alphabet a child traced after being told she was not meant to read.

I was born in the archive’s dust, which is not dust but the powdered bones of questions. I was born when the archivist lifted a glove and the dead began to gossip. I was born from an index card: Female, age unknown, condition: valuable. I was born from the word unknown until unknown split open and spilled generations of black-eyed peas, train whistles, river mud, milk teeth, Sunday hats.

I was born during a storm the newspapers did not mention. I was born in a shotgun house with both doors open, so the spirit could pass clean through. I was born under the sign of the mule and the star, of the tambourine and the flood, of the baby who arrives already carrying the grandmother. I was born crying like a harmonica dropped down a well.

I was born again when my mother told the story differently. I was born again when my grandmother corrected her. I was born again when the aunties said both of them were lying and then sang the truth into the beans. I was born in contradiction, swaddled in rumor, rocked by a chair that had never belonged to anyone free and yet kept rocking.

I was born with cotton in my ears and a trumpet in my chest. I was born in the hush arbor, in the storefront church, in the schoolhouse with patched windows, in the train station where departures bloomed like bruises. I was born in the Great Migration’s suitcase beside a Bible, a biscuit, a pistol, a photograph of somebody who stayed.

I was born in a birth certificate amended by thunder. I was born in the blank line for father, the smudged line for mother, the official seal pressed down like a thumb on the soft head of morning. I was born and the state looked away. I was born and the women looked closer.

I was born from water, from rupture, from witness. I was born from somebody’s prayer under somebody else’s whip. I was born from the terrible arithmetic of survival: one child hidden, one song coded, one road north, one root carried in the hem. I was born where the past is not past but a wet nurse, a bloodhound, a lantern, a mirror.

I was born, I was born, I was born—each time less alone. I was born in the scattered pages and the missing pages and the pages burned warm in the stove. I was born in the story that cannot be cataloged, only carried. I was born with my ear to the ground, listening to the unborn rehearse my name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental first-person literary collage in the style of a catalog of origins, using anaphora, historical echoes, and strange domestic images like skillets, lye, coffee grounds, eggshells, and rivers.
counterfactuals.output:
I was born from the skillet left black on the stove, from its moon of grease, from the little weather of salt, from the iron remembering every hand that had ever lifted it.

I was born from lye, from the white bite of it, from soap hardening in a wooden mold, from my grandmother’s warning: don’t touch what cleans you.

I was born from coffee grounds in the sink, dark as a map of failed countries, dark as the mouths of soldiers in photographs, dark as the soil that received the names nobody wrote down.

I was born from eggshells cracked against a chipped bowl, each one a small ruined parliament, each one a white helmet, each one holding for a moment the wet sun of breakfast.

I was born from the river before it had a bridge, from the bridge before it had a war, from the war before it had a monument, from the monument before it had pigeons and schoolchildren and a plaque no one could pronounce without lying.

I was born from the cupboard of rags.

I was born from the census.

I was born from the hand that counted me incorrectly.

I was born from a woman boiling linens at dawn, her face bright with steam, her back bent like a question mark the century refused to answer. She stirred the sheets with a broom handle. She stirred the fever out. She stirred the blood out. She stirred the empire out as much as she could.

I was born from flour in a blue tin, from the spoon standing upright in beans, from the onion sprouting green spears in the dark, from the mouse caught under a teacup and the child praying for its escape.

I was born saying: here is the beginning.

I was born saying: no, before that.

I was born saying: before that, too.

Before the house, the ash. Before the ash, the tree. Before the tree, the river dragging stones in its sleep. Before the river, rain entering the mouths of animals. Before the animals, a pressure, a heat, a blackness with no furniture.

Still, I keep finding furniture.

A chair with one leg shorter than history.

A bed that remembers every birth as a kind of weather.

A table where the dead sit down first.

I was born from the apron pocket: string, thimble, receipt, match, tooth, key. I was born from the key that opened nothing by the time it reached me. I was born from the nothing it opened: a room of blue dust, a window swollen shut, a wasp’s nest in the rafters like a paper heart.

I was born from a country that changed its name while the soup was cooling.

I was born from a border drawn through a cabbage patch.

I was born from papers folded into oilcloth and hidden under loose floorboards.

I was born from the loose floorboards.

I was born from the squeak that betrayed us.

At night the kettle ticks itself empty. The skillet cools. The sink exhales its metallic creek. In the drain, coffee grounds gather like refugees at a station, each grain carrying a bitter passport, each grain stamped with morning.

I was born from bitterness.

I was born from morning.

I was born from the rooster painted on the plate and the actual rooster slaughtered behind the shed. From the ax rinsed in the rain barrel. From the feathers stuck to the wrist. From the child watching through the screen door, learning that hunger has a ceremony.

I was born from ceremony without priests.

I was born from priests without mercy.

I was born from mercy hiding in a heel of bread.

Listen: the river is still under the floor. It moves through the pipes, through the laundry, through the blue veins of the wrist. It carries eggshells, soap flakes, hair, a button, a battlefield, a lullaby, the ash from a stove no one has lit in fifty years.

I cup my hands and drink.

It tastes of iron. It tastes of names. It tastes of the first skillet cooling in the first kitchen after the first exile, when someone said we are safe now, and someone else, already sweeping, said not yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, lyrical paragraph beginning with “I was born,” where the speaker seems to be many people at once and references themes of race, gender, superstition, burden, and twentieth-century identity.
counterfactuals.output: I was born, it seems, in several doorways at once: under a black moon and a white ceiling, in a girl’s cry and a boy’s clenched fist, in the kitchen where salt was thrown over shoulders and in the street where names were thrown like stones; I carried my grandmother’s Bible, my father’s silence, my mother’s iron, the red thread against the evil eye, the census mark, the factory number, the lipstick, the lash, the burden of being seen and mis-seen in the hard electric century that promised freedom through wires and war; I was the maid and the soldier, the exile and the citizen, the daughter taught to lower her eyes, the son taught never to weep, the body darkened into symbol, lightened into permission, divided by mirrors yet multiplied by every gaze that tried to fix me; I walked through radios, ration lines, dance halls, courtrooms, back doors, front lines, beauty parlors, and burning towns, wearing other people’s fears like inherited coats, while omens fluttered in the rafters and history pressed its thumb against my tongue, asking me to speak as one and answer as many.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic monologue made entirely of uncanny birth statements, blending biblical references, abolitionist/feminist echoes, Southern gothic imagery, and archival language.
counterfactuals.output:
I was born in the ledger before I was born in the flesh.

I was born between “begat” and “behold,” where the family tree split like lightning over a burnt field.

I was born under a black sun, with the midwife reading Exodus by the light of a mule’s blind eye.

I was born in the cotton’s white whisper, not picked but summoned, not delivered but filed.

I was born from a mother who had no legal name, only marks, margins, inventory, breath.

I was born when the Red Sea opened in a courthouse drawer and every drowned chariot became a receipt.

I was born saying, Ain’t I, before I knew what I was.

I was born with a question in my mouth and a nail in the door.

I was born of woman, and of woman’s labor, and of woman’s refusal to be measured in bushels, births, or bruises.

I was born in the year of our Lord crossed out, rewritten, and sealed with mildew.

I was born where the magnolia rotted sweetly over the graves of children whose names were borrowed, bartered, or erased.

I was born with Eve’s rib in my fist and Hagar’s wilderness in my throat.

I was born behind the smokehouse, where the hymn climbed crooked and the moon hung like a wet sheet.

I was born from an affidavit sworn by a trembling hand.

I was born Exhibit A, child of Sorrow, daughter of No Further Record.

I was born after the auction bell, before the rooster, during the hour when ghosts count the living.

I was born with Moses hidden in the rushes of my hair.

I was born with Pharaoh’s tally on my ankle and a river rehearsing my escape.

I was born in a cabin that leaned like a witness afraid to testify.

I was born under Spanish moss that kept the secrets of women who stitched freedom into hems.

I was born from a scream pressed flat between pages.

I was born from the wet ink of emancipation, still shackled to the clerk’s dry tongue.

I was born where the plantation house stared through its broken windows and called itself heritage.

I was born a footnote, then a fire.

I was born in the attic with the dead brides, the rusted cradle, the hymnals swollen by floodwater.

I was born in the margin marked “female,” where the law put its thumb and the spirit bit through.

I was born with Sojourner’s thunder in my spine and a broom of prophecy at the door.

I was born asking whether my body was a nation, a burden, a battlefield, or a bell.

I was born from Sarah’s laughter turned bitter, from Mary’s yes made dangerous, from Rachel weeping past the county line.

I was born beneath a sky the color of old bruises and open Bibles.

I was born when the blood on the lintel spelled my grandmother’s first unrecorded name.

I was born in the census, aged zero, race noted, mother unknown, value disputed.

I was born from the hush after the whip, from the hush before the uprising, from the hush women used to sharpen knives.

I was born with milk in one hand and a manifesto in the other.

I was born in a graveyard of unmarked mothers, each stone a locked mouth, each root a witness.

I was born from the cellar’s damp gospel, where jars of peaches glowed like preserved suns.

I was born when the angel passed over and forgot to spare the master’s house from memory.

I was born carrying a birth certificate made of quilt scraps, ash, and testimony.

I was born not once but recorded many times: as issue, increase, property, girl, contraband, freedwoman, wife, widow, claimant, deceased.

I was born from the crack in the overseer’s whip where lightning entered history.

I was born with a psalm stitched under my tongue and a curse buried under the porch.

I was born in the storm cellar while the hounds sang genealogies.

I was born where the well gave back faces instead of water.

I was born to a mother who labored like a prophet and bled like a treaty.

I was born from the blackened rafters of a church that kept praising after the fire.

I was born with Judith’s blade beneath my pillow and Deborah’s palm tree growing through my ribs.

I was born in the notation “illegible,” and there I learned to shine.

I was born when the archive sneezed dust and called it evidence.

I was born from a box labeled Miscellaneous Negro Papers, tied with red string like an umbilical cord.

I was born before the witness could sign, after the witness had vanished, during the witness’s eternal return.

I was born in the South’s open mouth, where sweetness fermented into rot and rot into song.

I was born under a porch where a doll with no eyes kept rocking itself.

I was born in the seam between amen and revolt.

I was born from a mother who said, This child is mine, though the world wrote otherwise.

I was born with the mark of Cain on the hand that counted me.

I was born with the mark of God on the hand that freed me.

I was born from the first breath after no.

I was born from every woman who stood in a doorway and became the door.

I was born with my caul full of moonwater, court orders, and crow feathers.

I was born singing Go Down, Moses to a room of men who preferred silence.

I was born when the plantation bell cracked and sounded like my name.

I was born of dust, yes, but dust that remembered being star, road, bone, and witness.

I was born from a womb the archive could not own.

I was born, and the house began to rot from the portrait frames inward.

I was born, and the Bible fell open to deliverance.

I was born, and the ledger bled.

I was born, and the dead women rose to count me themselves.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness prose poem with the repeated refrain “I was born,” full of disjointed literary references, haunting rural objects, and lines that feel borrowed from many old books.
counterfactuals.output:
I was born, and the rain was already speaking in the broken Latin of the gutters, and the fields leaned close like old women who had read too much scripture and remembered none of it correctly. I was born in a room with a blue pitcher, a cracked basin, a fly circling the lamp as if it were the last sun, and somewhere a cowbell saying no, no, no to the dusk.

I was born, though perhaps it was only a rumor in a parish register, ink gone brown as apple-skin, a name scratched beside a date, a witness with dirt under his nails. The midwife smelled of fennel and iron. The bedposts were dark as judges. Outside, the orchard stood in its wet boots, holding up its blossoms like little torn letters from the dead.

I was born into the house of the stopped clock, the rusted key, the Bible with pressed moths in the pages, the wooden spoon worn thin as a saint’s wrist. I was born among the hens and the winter cabbage, among the scythes hung in the shed like crescent moons confiscated from some defeated kingdom. I was born, and the black dog at the threshold lifted his head as if he knew me from another century.

I was born after the hero had gone to sea, before the governess heard the step in the corridor, while the poor clerk warmed his fingers over a candle and the mad wife laughed behind the wallpaper. I was born in the margin, where the printer’s ink blotted and the footnote lost its nerve. I was born under a sentence that had been translated too many times: behold, alas, nevertheless, and all the ships departed.

I was born, and the well had a stone lip, and the bucket came up brimming with sky. The corncrib whispered in its sleep. The scarecrow wore my father’s coat and my mother’s sorrow. In the barn, a ladder ascended nowhere, rung by rung into the swallows. I was born with burrs in my blanket and a piece of red thread tied around my wrist to keep away whatever had already entered.

I was born in the season of unripe plums, when the road was a yellow ribbon of dust and the chapel bell sounded as if struck underwater. Someone was always leaving: the peddler with his tin cups, the soldier with his polished buttons, the sister with her little valise, the soul with its candle-end of breath. I was born, and every door in the county learned to sigh on its hinges.

I was born with a taste for forbidden rooms, for attics where trunks exhale camphor and grief, for portraits whose eyes follow not you but someone standing behind you. I was born beside the spinning wheel, the mildewed quilt, the cradle that rocked once by itself and then was still. The moon put her white hand through the window. The fox crossed the yard carrying a mouthful of feathers like a prophecy.

I was born, I was born, I was born—each time farther from the village, nearer the black trees, nearer the book that writes itself after midnight. A raven misquoted the prophets from the fencepost. The pond held its breath beneath a skin of green. In the pantry, onions sprouted pale antlers. In the cellar, jars of peaches glowed like captive afternoons, sweet and sealed and already gone.

I was born from the scratch of a quill, from the soot of a chimney, from the dust beneath a marriage bed. I was born where the lane bends and the child vanishes in stories told too often; where the horse’s skull lies half-buried by the hedge; where the milk turns in thunder; where the dead are careful not to wake the living. I was born, and the old books opened their mouths, but what came out was wind, chaff, a handful of names, and the long grass bending.
